text: One was strict, stubborn and obsessed with discipline. They called him the General.
The other was a skinny kid from the streets near the Ajax stadium who argued with everyone, about everything.
Together, they invented a new kind of football. Then they brought it to Barcelona — not once, but twice.
This is the story of Rinus Michels and Johan Cruyff, side by side.
Part one. Two Amsterdam boys.
Rinus Michels was born in Amsterdam in nineteen twenty-eight. Before he ever coached, he was a centre-forward for Ajax, strong and direct, and he played for the Netherlands.
Johan Cruyff was born in Amsterdam nineteen years later, a few streets from the Ajax ground. He was at the club almost before he could read.
In January nineteen sixty-five, the two lives crossed. Michels became Ajax's coach. Cruyff was seventeen, and already in the first team.
Michels found a club that trained part-time. He turned it into a professional machine: double sessions, endless running, iron discipline.
And at the centre of it he put the boy who hated being told what to do.
They argued constantly. But Michels understood that Cruyff saw the pitch like no one else — and Cruyff understood that Michels could build a team around that vision.
Ajax went from a struggling club to the best team in the Netherlands. In nineteen sixty-nine, they reached the European Cup final.
Part two. Total football.
That first final, in Madrid, was a lesson. AC Milan beat Ajax four–one.
Michels went back to work. Players learned to swap positions, to press as a group, to make the pitch big when they had the ball and small when they didn't.
Two years later, at Wembley, Ajax were champions of Europe.
The world would call it total football: every player able to attack, defend and think. Michels designed it. Cruyff conducted it, from the middle of the pitch.
Part three. Barcelona, together.
Then, in nineteen seventy-one, the teacher left. Michels accepted an offer from FC Barcelona.
Two years later, the student followed. In August nineteen seventy-three, Cruyff flew to Barcelona to play for Michels again.
In their first season together in Spain, Barça won the league for the first time in fourteen years — and beat Real Madrid five–nil at the Bernabéu along the way.
That summer, the Netherlands asked Michels to lead them at the World Cup — while he was still Barça's coach.
So the Barcelona coach and Barcelona's star went to West Germany together, in orange.
Their team became the sensation of the tournament.
They lost the final, two–one to West Germany.
But they came home as heroes — and as the team that showed the world how football would be played for the next fifty years.
Michels left Barça in nineteen seventy-five, and came back for a second spell in nineteen seventy-six.
Cruyff was still there. It wasn't always easy — two strong personalities rarely are.
In nineteen seventy-eight, Barça won the Spanish Cup. That summer, both men left the club. The first chapter of the Dutch Barça was over.
Part four. Two roads.
In the eighties, the two men went different ways. Michels coached in Germany, at Cologne, and then became the most powerful figure in Dutch football, at the national federation.
Cruyff played on — in America, in Spain, then back at Ajax and Feyenoord. In nineteen eighty-five, he became Ajax's coach. Now the student was a teacher.
In nineteen eighty-five, Michels also had heart surgery. Many thought his coaching days were over.
Part five. Nineteen eighty-eight.

Then came nineteen eighty-eight — the year both of them reached their peak again. In June, Michels led the Netherlands to the European Championship, the country's first major trophy, with Gullit, Van Basten, Rijkaard and Koeman.
And that same summer, Cruyff went back to Barcelona — this time as coach.
He brought Michels's ideas with him, and added his own: even more possession, even more risk, and young players trusted from the academy. Four years later, Barça won their first European Cup.
In nineteen ninety-nine, FIFA named Rinus Michels the coach of the century. He died in two thousand and five.
Cruyff died in twenty sixteen. Today, the stadium where Barça's women and young players play bears his name.

People often argue about which of them mattered more. Maybe that's the wrong question. Michels created the idea. Cruyff turned it into a club's identity. Without the teacher, there is no student — and without the student, the lesson might have been forgotten.
Who do you think mattered more to Barça — the teacher or the student? Tell me in the comments.
